subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR ECONOMIC MEASURES, PLANNED INVESTMENT AND FOREIGN OWNERSHIP POLICIES TO ACHIEVE HIGH EMPLOYMENT THROUGH DEVELOPMENT OF SECONDARY MANUFACTURING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this government will be known to history as the government that gambled and lost. Cold bloodedly and deliberately it has gambled on taking measures the textbooks prescribed to cut down inflation. It knew perfectly well that such a massive slowdown of the economy would cause massive unemployment. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said he could live with 6 per cent unemployment. The chairman of the Prices and Incomes Commission subsequently told a university audience that he and others knew that the unemployed would bear the brunt of the fight against inflation. But this gambling govern-

May 18, 1971
Measures to Improve Economy ment went ahead trying to cure inflation by massive doses of unemployment. They gambled with the economy and lost.
In March their own member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) told the House that the government's policies to deal with unemployment and inflation had been a near economic disaster and a total moral disaster. While there had been a more modest rate of price increases as a result- and I may say a temporary result-the main beneficiaries of the exercise, he said, had been the people with money, and those who had suffered were the unemployed. Young Canadians, too, have suffered, he said, pointing out that last year's economic slowdown resulted in lost economic activity of $3.5 billion, an amount which, if it had been properly spent, could have provided the base for 100,000 new jobs.
But the government did not limit its reckless activities to the economy. It has gambled and is still gambling with the lives of 22 million Canadians. This government, in spite of its show of bravado, is losing ground steadily. But its loss is as nothing compared with the losses being sustained by the Canadian people. The plight of the elderly, the sick, the handicapped, the veterans, those on low fixed incomes, families on social assistance, and the unemployed is tragic and deepening with every move this gambling government makes.
Today, I want to speak particularly of the cost to young people from coast to coast. They are suffering now and because of their situation our whole Canadian future is in danger. Last fall there were plenty of warnings given after the summer we went through. Dr. Baetz of the Canadian Social Development Council gave figures to indicate that most likely there would be larger numbers of unemployed again this summer. His figures were underestimations. The figures for April of this year showed an 11,000 reduction in the number of unemployed aged 55 years or more, but a sharp increase in the number of younger workers looking for jobs. For those under 25 years, the seasonally adjusted rate of unemployment went up from 11.1 per cent in March to 12.3 per cent in April, and there were 57,000 more of them unemployed in April than there were a year ago.
As already mentioned in this debate, Arthur Smith, Chairman of the Economic Council of Canada, has warned that unemployment will be excessive for at least three years. Last year's figures showed a large number of unemployed young people. A release issued at the end of summer by the Department of Manpower showed that of
179,000	students registered across Canada for employment at the peak of summer, 68 per cent of them found jobs, 32 per cent were still seeking work, and of these 27 per cent were post-secondary students and 73 per cent were high school students. It was the high school students who had to bear the brunt of the unemployment catastrophe.
That was the situation last summer. The picture now has become even more sombre, because this year unemployment has reached up into the ranks of college graduates. It got there last year but is making a heavier impact this year. In April, a report was issued by the Science Council of Canada, not a rabble rousing body but a group of people who consider themselves to be very cautious and careful in the figures they use. This is what the report said in essence:
Half of the 14,000 or so students graduating from Canadian universities in science and engineering this year will not be "effectively utilized," according to a study prepared for the Science Council of Canada.
This figure includes graduates at the bachelor's, master's and Ph.D. level.
About 400 of the 1,200 to 1,500 post-graduate students who will receive PhD's this year could be in surplus.
Prospects for PhD's next year are bleaker. The most optimistic prediction is that 500 of the 1,800 science and engineering PhD's will be in surplus.
The outlook for the next few years is just as gloomy.
In the face of this, I do not see how there can be such whistling in the dark in such a cheerful way by members on the government benches. It is another case where there are none so blind as those who will not see, and none so deaf as those who will not hear. It is no longer just the problem of summer employment for young people that is in front of us. The cold truth of the matter is that society no longer has a place for growing numbers of young people. Under the government's policies young people are being discarded, like old cars on the junk heaps of industry. That is what has been happening to them.
I can tell hon. members on the government benches what is happening. I will take my own province of British Columbia as an example. In a memorandum dated April 8 of this year to the Vancouver City Council dealing with the subject of single transients, aged 18 to 25 years, in British Columbia, the Board of Administration reported some chilling facts.
In 1965 the 25 and under age group represented 2.5 per cent of the total population in receipt of social assistance. By 1970, this 18 to 25 year old population represented 11.4 per cent of the total receiving social assistance, an increase of almost 500 per cent in the five year period.
Population figures for British Columbia show that in the next five years there wil be a peak population of 203,000 aged 15 to 19 as compared with the present population in this age group of 182,400.
What is going to happen to the social assistance figures for British Columbia? What is going to happen to the social assistance figures for every municipality across Canada? What is going to happen to the taxpayers' ability to foot the bill? More important, what is going to happen to our young people? What is going to happen to our society? In this connection studies have been going on in British Columbia for some time, and they show what is happening right now. I can tell hon. members opposite the sort of thing that is going on now, and what their policies are doing to the young people of this country.
These studies in my own city of Vancouver show that a new style of life has been evolving for some time, a welfare life style among young people. It already is affecting about 15 per cent of a large sample of the
[Mrs. Maclnnis.j
May 18, 1971

population, young men and young women alike. These are young people who have been without work over the last months and years, and these are some of the things that the survey is finding out about them. This rot will spread because nothing is being done to check it.
This 15 per cent of our young people no longer want full-time work. Many no longer want work of any kind. They have learned to live on welfare, on a marginal income because they have no opportunity for work, and now they are used to living on welfare. Most of them are using drugs on a daily basis. They include young people from all levels of education, including university graduates. Half of them are living communally, or I suppose you could call it wholesale common-law. Most of them come from homes above the poverty level. This last fact is something which should strike home to hon. members opposite who are inclined to think that as long as the comfortable sector of society is doing well, we are living in the best of all worlds and God's in his heaven. These are young people for whom there is no place in our society. They no longer have a role in the community. They have no chance to earn their own way. They have no chance for responsibility. Without responsibility what is going to happen even to their rights as human beings?
We know that Mayor Campbell of Vancouver dismisses them as free-loaders and hopes for a bigger budget for law and order to handle what may result. We know that our provincial Minister of Rehabilitation-what a word that is to apply to P. A. Gaglardi!-believes in posting notices telling young people to stay away from British Columbia. If this continues, I suppose we shall soon find each province putting up a Chinese wall around itself, not only for chicken and egg wars but to keep out young Canadians for whom there is no work. Yet the federal government sings its soul to glory, and says we have turned the comer, that we are taking more ore out of the ground, that we are having more export trade, that everything is wonderful. But, Mr. Speaker, at the heart of this country the most important thing is that we have no place for our young people. I am talking about people. Hon. members opposite can talk about the rest of things if they like, but let me warn them that once young people have lost confidence it does not matter what hon. gentlemen opposite do with the ore, the minerals and the export trade. Their government is finished.
An hon. member opposite has said that the Canadian people should have confidence in the government. Do you expect them to have confidence in a government that carries on in this way, a government that just does not care? I see the minister nodding his head affirmatively. I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, but I must conclude that not only has he no ears and no eyes but that his heart has been replaced with something a great deal more chilly than a human heart ought to be.
In a statement on income security issued in April by the National Council of Welfare we find this sentence:
Updated estimates based on those prepared for the Carter Commission indicate that the cost to the taxpayer of indirect
Measures to Improve Economy
subsidies to the rich extended through the tax system alone is at least $800 million-one-third more than the entire family allowance program.
The Opportunities for Youth program and the other programs provided by this government, if my arithmetic is correct, will provide $82 million for unemployed youth this summer-$800 million as subsidies to the wealthy through our tax system and $82 million to the unemployed youth! It is not hard to see what should be done, Mr. Speaker. The government should cut out its widespread and unjust subsidization of those people who do not need it and should use their money to give young people the start they need.
It has been pointed out this afternoon that in order to achieve anything substantial we would have to cut our standard of living down to something akin to what exists in the nether regions of Africa. But some of us have memories of what happened when World War II came along, Mr. Speaker. Until then there had been no money for anything, but because we had a government that decided the war had to be proceeded with, suddenly we had growth and industry and all the things necessary to pursue that war. If we had the kind of government that did not have twisted and crooked values, if we had the kind that cared about people and not just the affluent elite, there would be no difficulty about putting people to work. We would clean up pollution, clean up the beaches; we would build schools, establish forests and do the other things that this country needs. We would fill the cultural gap that is so obvious in Canada and we would replan and rebuild our cities into places decent enough for people to live in.
When we say these things out loud, members of the government shake their heads and say, "We have heard nothing new". They are not new but then they are as new as Christianity in that it has never been tried. I think the government should try some of these suggestions before they say there is nothing new. Until they do we will have the young people of this country undermining the values of our society because they must.

May 18. 1971
Measures to Improve Economy GOVERNMENT ORDERS BUSINESS OF SUPPLY

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Saltsman:
That this House calls upon the government to adopt immediate emergency economic measures to move the economy to high employment through special programs and more expansionary monetary and fiscal policies, and also to achieve full potential growth through a planned investment and foreign ownership policy and to stimulate the development of secondary manufacturing as the only way of providing the necessary employment opportunities for the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who enter the work force every year.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR ECONOMIC MEASURES, PLANNED INVESTMENT AND FOREIGN OWNERSHIP POLICIES TO ACHIEVE HIGH EMPLOYMENT THROUGH DEVELOPMENT OF SECONDARY MANUFACTURING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in support of the motion before us on the subject of economic conditions. I believe that we need to adopt a more expansionary philosophy in connection with our monetary and fiscal policies, particularly now that so many people are unemployed. I congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) upon expressing her concern for people. The sad part is that much of what she said is true. I am not going to deal with the question of unemployment rates as the Leader of the Official Opposition dealt with them at length.
I should like to take a brief look at what has gone on in Canada in the last five of six years. We have seen Mr. Trudeau and Mr. Benson parrying on an experiment to find out whether a country the size of Canada could control inflation and to learn what the net result of it would be. In looking at Canada's economic picture from 1965 to 1968, we find that this country had the highest rate of inflation in what might be called the western world. I believe only The Netherlands exceeded Canada's rate of inflation during that period. That was because they had just recently removed the wage and price controls in that country.
From July 1968 until December 1970, Canada had the lowest rate of inflation in the western world, so we went from a period of sharply accelerated inflation to a period of very low inflation-in fact, no inflation at all. I think the rate for the last full year was 1.9 per cent and perhaps this is good. Perhaps the government should be patted on the back. They attempted to do this themselves on January 1, 1971, when the Prime Minister said that he had inflation licked. But what did he say a year earlier on January 1, 1970? He said that we would have to live with unemployment and that even if it got above 6 per cent we would still have to live with it. He was determined to control or curtail inflation. What effect did this sharp reduction of inflation have in Canada from June 1968 to the end of 1970? Well, we had an influx of foreign moneys. The dollar seeks a place where it can find the highest rate of return, so dollars came to Canada. We still kept a tight monetary policy and we had to float our dollar or it would have cost us an
enormous amount of money to pay the difference in exchange.
Floating the Canadian dollar cost us, as primary producers and producers of manufactured goods, millions of dollars. And was it necessary? What was the net result of this curtailed rate of growth, this curtailed monetary policy? The Prime Minister indicated the result last week on the television program "Weekend" when he said:
... the Canadian dollar is so strong indeed that it is hurting our export trade because people are finding it cheaper to import goods and more difficult to sell them abroad.
What does this mean to the Canadian seeking work? It creates a situation where it is cheaper to buy goods that come into Canada and it is more difficult to sell the goods produced in Canada, therefore our export total goes down and our import total goes up. Of course, this creates unemployment. Perhaps Mr. Smith of the Economic Council of Canada was correct when, in the fifth or sixth report of that council, he said that Canada really cannot control its rate of inflation and if we do perhaps it will cause undue hardship on various segments of our society. Unpalatable as that statement may be, I think it must be reckoned with and we have to accept portions of it. What portion of the Canadian economy can Canadians control? What portion of the monetary policy of Canada can Canadians control?
First of all, I think Canada should control the rate of differential between the Canadian dollar and the American dollar, the mark, the yen or whatever it might be. We can control that, and we should make a determined effort to see that our dollar should be 8 per cent, 10 per cent or 5 per cent less in value than the American dollar. In this country we are faced with a different cost of production. We produce for a small home market. We produce mainly in a winter climate and therefore we should have a differential of about 8 per cent between our dollar and the American dollar. In doing this, we must recognize that we have to allow our dollar to inflate at a rate similar to the currencies in the rest of the western world, particularly the United States dollar.
It is well known that a crisis developed because the value fixed for our currency was out of line with the value that the free forces of the market would have established. That is why Germany recently, after having gone through a similar period, has had to float its currency. I think that we need a basic expansionary policy which will allow our money supply to expand. It is interesting to note that even although we have gone through a two-year period of tight money in this country, the government is still wondering which is worse, unemployment or inflation. Last month, I think, the Prime Minister issued a grave warning that we were not to permit another inflationary spiral to take place.
Actually, Canada is a country that can be hurt in two ways. If we permit our economy to inflate too fast, we shall price ourselves out of world markets. On the other hand, if our fiscal policies are too restrictive, our money will increase in value and we shall, as well, price our-

May 18, 1971

selves out of world markets. In that sense, as I say, we can price ourselves out of world markets. We must not allow our economy to inflate too quickly and neither must we embark on too stringent a monetary policy. I think it has been accepted that we must try to balance the scales in that regard.
Whether you judge the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) in a political or non-political sense, you will see that he has failed to balance the economy and to keep in step with the rest of the world. Here, he has failed miserably. He brought about a period of high inflation prior to 1968; that priced us out of world markets. Then he tried to curtail inflation too rapidly between 1968 and 1970 and, since it became cheaper to import goods than to produce our own, we were also priced out of the market. Our money became more valuable and that increased the price of our products in world markets. Both actions have brought the same result.
It is no wonder that the hon. member for Duvemay (Mr. Kierans), who was formerly minister in charge of the Post Office, resigned. He became thoroughly disgusted with the inept job the Minister of Finance is doing. In other words, he passed judgment on the government. He had given advice to the Minister of Finance. One could read the speech that the hon. member gave on June 2, 1970. He recognized, on June 2, that the Canadian dollar was strong and far stronger than the American dollar. If I had time I would read what he said in that speech about the floating of the Canadian dollar. He recognized that if we were not careful, we could price ourselves out of world markets, especially if we adopted too stringent a monetary policy.
It is interesting to note what Mr. Rasminsky, head of the Bank of Canada, had to say about this matter. The Toronto Telegram of Friday, April 30, contained this report:
Mr. Rasminsky's position on the direction of economic policy is this: Economic growth should be geared to ensure a steady reduction in unemployment while simultaneously 'avoiding an expansion so rapid that it would over-shoot the mark.'
In other words, he recognizes clearly this question of balance. We must maintain this balance which involves on the one hand our own economic and monetary policy and, on the other, the actions of those with whom we trade. Canada really is a major trading nation. In British Columbia, the Prime Minister said that almost 50 per cent of our goods are exported. I think the figure is higher than that. I think probably about 70 per cent of Canadian production, either directly or indirectly, is export oriented. Our monetary policy, in other words, must keep in step with that of our trading partners, basically the countries of the western world. The Minister of Finance has failed miserably to accomplish this. If we had kept in step we would not have needed to float our dollar, unless he wanted our dollar to come up to par with the United States dollar. I have not heard him say that. On the other hand, I have heard him say that he wants our dollar to be worth 95 cents or less in terms of the United States dollar. He ought to be taking steps to do that and he is not doing so.
Measures to Improve Economy
The Prime Minister is still caught up in his fears about inflation. He wonders which is best, high employment and high inflation or high unemployment and no inflation. You cannot state the problem that simply. We have to consider the rest of the world. If there is inflation in the rest of the world, surely we need some inflation in Canada, although I should like to think of it as being lower than that in the rest of the world. Otherwise, our dollar would become too strong and we would price ourselves out of world markets in that way, as well. We can clearly see that we have been out of step with our trading partners in the western world. We must get in step with them, because a great deal of Canada's employment depends on export projects.
Why does this country which is capable of producing a great deal depend so much on exports? We do not have to depend on exports. The fact of the matter is that we can buy imports more cheaply than the goods we can produce here. So, we must get in step with the rest of the world so that Canadians can be induced to buy Canadian produced goods and so that Canadian produced goods have a chance in the markets of the world. The Minister of Finance has failed in that Canada's monetary policy has not kept in step with policies prevailing in the rest of the world. He has failed miserably in creating an economic climate in Canada in which the current work force will be absorbed in the economy and in which the increase in the labour force, an increase resulting from the natural rate of growth in this country, will be absorbed in the economy. To my way of thinking that is the most serious charge to be made against the minister. I commend the hon. member for Duvernay for resigning from the cabinet. In doing so he pointed out vividly to the Canadian people that all was not well with our economic policies and that action ought to be taken.
I urge the Canadian people who are to go to the polls on May 31 in the four by-elections to register their disgust with the way the Canadian government has managed their economic affairs. One could talk about monetary policy all day; that really does not touch the imaginations of many of the little people throughout Canada. On the other hand, the subject does touch the pocketbooks of many of our little people and, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) so aptly put it, government policies have detracted from the opportunities of young people to become part of the growing and viable economy that we ought to have in Canada. I severely condemn the Minister of Finance because of his inept handling of the Canadian economy and economic policy in the past two years.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR ECONOMIC MEASURES, PLANNED INVESTMENT AND FOREIGN OWNERSHIP POLICIES TO ACHIEVE HIGH EMPLOYMENT THROUGH DEVELOPMENT OF SECONDARY MANUFACTURING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 18, 1971, with June around the corner and July and August in our immediate future, with September looming, that being the month in which we begin to see lay-offs in small industries and decreasing employment opportunities, with the temperatures in the seventies and the prospect of temperatures rising to the eight-ties. we should not be talking about unemployment. It was no consolation to Canadians who listened to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) today to hear that he

May 18, 1971
Measures to Improve Economy blamed unemployment on God and on a late spring. First, it is not correct that we have had a late spring. Actually, in those areas where we have the worst unemployment at the moment, spring has been at least one month early. I was astounded to learn this week that the regional director for the Atlantic region said there was excessive unemployment in that area because of the late spring. He knows that is not correct, and he knows that spring this year has been relatively early.
It was little consolation to listen to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on national television on Sunday night talking about the reasons behind government policies of about one year ago. He suggested that they created the situation we have today. The Prime Minister suggested that Canada had to opt for an anti-inflationary policy because inflation and the runaway effects of inflation would have such a detrimental effect on unemployment. Of all the countries, the minister used Latin America as an example. He said that we can see what is happening in Latin America. He tried to create the impression that today inflation in Canada had reached such devastating proportions that it had to be brought under control at all costs. Second, he indicated that because we are an exporting nation largely dependent on exports to the United States and other countries, inflation had to be checked. Third, he indicated that the reason it had to be checked was its effect on the little man, people on fixed incomes, seasonally employed, on pensions and people who receive $250 or $300 a month on which to raise a family. These are the people who will be hurt if inflation is not brought under control.
The fallacies are simple. The Prime Minister and his government have created the demon of inflation. Inflation had never reached the proportions it reached in Canada in 1970. We never had to create massive unemployment to bring it under control. The Prime Minister created the feeling of "Trudeauphobia" and the fear of inflation in order to justify the sad state of affairs, as well as the selection of very serious and chronic economic policies.
The minister referred to the export situation. We all know that if we have inflation at the rate of 10 per cent a year and our neighbours have inflation at the rate of 5 per cent a year, we are hurting our export markets. The fact is that our greatest export market, the United States, had an inflationary rate of 6 per cent last year. We had a rate of 1.5 per cent. I am no economist, but it is simple logic that the aim of Canada should be to keep inflation in harmony with that in the nations to which we export our produce in order to remain competitive. The fact is that it is a comparative problem.
Another fallacy is that the very people the Prime Minister wants to help with his anti-inflation policies, those on fixed incomes, seasonally and marginally employed and the unemployed, are the people who have been most adversely affected. They have been rendered unemployed. Members opposite know that this is a fact.
The results of the present policies have been massive unemployment, an increase in regional disparity, much
more difficulty in trying to export the unfinished resource products of the agricultural industry, the forest industry including the paper industry, the fishing industry and the mining industry. All those areas which differ from the more industrialized regions of Canada, such as the Atlantic region, Quebec, and the northern prairie region and parts of British Columbia are the areas that have been most adversely affected.
We have had a tremendous loss in potential. If members had time to ponder this fact, they would see the effect which this loss of potential had on Canada. If an industry is forced to cut back, lay off and produce at a slower rate, it has to charge more in order to increase its margin of profit. Everyone knows the effect that has on inflation. It is impossible for any member to develop the extent of the problem in 15 minutes. In the few minutes which I have, I want to dwell on some suggestions. I have been advised by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) that he will at least read these recommendations.
First, the minister should seriously consider abdicating his role as Minister of Finance. I do not believe that the minister has confidence in his policies. In fact, I do not believe they are his policies. I believe that the Prime Minister is cramming these policies down the throats of the cabinet members. Like the Canadian people, whether they like it or lump it, they have to swallow them. The Minister of Finance ought to be honourable and consider abdicating his present role.
Second, it is time that the Prime Minister assumed his responsibility and stated what the Canadian government, now in power with 152 members, has as its expectations for inflation and unemployment In Canada in 1971 and for successive years. Someone has to assume the responsibility of setting the goals and expectations for the Canadian nation. Will we tolerate 3 per cent inflation? Are we prepared to tolerate 6 per cent inflation? Are we prepared to tolerate 3 per cent unemployment? What are the goals the Canadian people can expect for 1971 and the successive years?
It is not good enough for the Prime Minister to appear on national television and ask the Canadian people to define what is meant by the term "full unemployment". This government which was elected by the Canadian people has the responsibility of setting the goals and expectations. If they are not prepared to do this, the least they can do is reduce expenditures $2 million by laying off Mr. Young and his bunch of boys who are running political interference for the government.
Third, the government should reassess its monetary and fiscal policies on a regional basis. I visited the province of Prince Edward Island last week. This month that province has 10.1 per cent unemployment on an actual unemployment basis. I believe that is the figure. The reason for this situation is that they cannot sell their agricultural produce to the New England market because of the tariff structure. The time has come when the government must realize that policies which are uniformly applied across Canada disadvantage some regions, especially the slow growth areas. We are the first to feel the pinch and slow down. We feel it to the greatest extent. We are the last to feel the effects of recovery.
[Mr. Lundrigan.l
May 18, 1971

Somebody has to face these facts, even though our small population does not justify it on a political basis.
Fourth, we must reassess our policy of incentives and loans to industry, especially in the slow growth areas. The three recent reports by the Minister of Finance and his parliamentary secretary bear me out on this. They indicate that in the slow growth areas, such as in the Atlantic regions, particular industries cannot avail themselves of the loans guaranteed by the government. The lending institutions refuse to co-operate. I am not saying the legislation is bad, but some way has to be found to enable industries to take fuller advantage of loan programs. If we expect these industries to recover, expand, grow and develop, we must make money available to them. The industries that And it most difficult to avail themselves of loans at the present time are the industries in the slow growth areas.
The major point I want to make is that the tax uncertainty in this nation has a crippling effect on our economy. People do not know where they are going. They do not know whether to expand. They do not know whether to take their few dollars out of the bank and invest them because they do not know when this valuation of assets will take place. They do not know about capital gains, the protective tariffs for small business and concessions to mining companies. All in all, the tax uncertainty is having a detrimental effect on the economy. The minister has been on the horns of a dilemma for a year in connection with these tax proposals. I am not prepared to wait for a month. Some indication has to be given of the present tax position of this government.
Another point is that the government must reassess its priorities. Many members religiously avoid mentioning the emphasis that is put today on linguistic equality in this nation. I continuously receive representations from concerned Canadian taxpayers on this matter. There is a tremendous effort being made in this country to bring about linguistic equality. On the west coast of the province of Newfoundland there is a place called Port au Port. The hon. member who represents that area can speak with authority on this. There is a very small group of people who live in that district who have been assimilated over the years. Now, this area has been classified as a bilingual district. Everything must be done on a bilingual basis, including the distribution of information. I believe it was in 1964 that Professor Stoker, a linguistic expert at the university, said that three years previously the process of assimilation had reached the stage where the people no longer had any desire to have a separate culture or anything of this nature. Yet that part of our country has been designated as a bilingual district.
Every day dozens of circulars and pieces of literature cross my desk. Whether we like it or not, they are printed in both languages. I can go further and state that there are civil servants taking language immersion courses who will retire before their courses are completed. There is no sense to this. I contend that a lot of problems in Canada, including Quebec, are economic, not language problems. I would like to see the present gov-
Measures to Improve Economy ernment reassess the problems and adopt some policy positions.
Ever since 1968 the Prime Minister of this country has acted like a great, charismatic leader on television, in this House and elsewhere. I have never heard him state in the House or publicly what he considers to be the priorities for this nation. I have never heard him state any clear, definitive policy positions. I have never heard him state any manpower policy positions. I have never heard him state any foreign-ownership policy positions. I have never heard him state any resource development policy position. This country cannot continue without being given some indication of over-all government policy.
You cannot kiss away the problems facing the Canadian nation at this moment. You cannot kiss away the unemployment problem facing Canada, the depression being experienced by the agricultural industry or the forest industry. Someone has to stand up and sanely, soberly and rationally lay down priorities and policy positions that are based on hard-nosed facts.
This is not a popularity contest that we are running, Mr. Speaker. Here we are in the month of May, and I suggest it is not enough for the Minister of Finance to tell the country that we are going to recover, that unemployment is going downhill. Are Canadians going to be satisfied come September when they have had only six weeks' work? I remind hon. gentlemen across the way that there are 659,000 Canadians out of work. Are they going to be satisfied, when the lay-offs start in September and the cold winter months are ahead of them, that this country is commencing a recovery? In my own province 16.4 per cent of the people are unemployed. This represents 25,000 people. This is the most diluted kind of statistic because the true figure may be more than 20 per cent. When people tell me that things are going to be better next week, I tell them that they are not better today. The Trudeaumania that swept this country in 1968 is fast becoming Trudeauphobia, and it is time we brought it to a stop.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR ECONOMIC MEASURES, PLANNED INVESTMENT AND FOREIGN OWNERSHIP POLICIES TO ACHIEVE HIGH EMPLOYMENT THROUGH DEVELOPMENT OF SECONDARY MANUFACTURING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the evidence that has been presented to members of this House in the past few days, and over the past several months in particular, demonstrates a total failure on the part of the government to deal with the problems facing the Canadian economy. I feel that the actions taken by the Liberal government can be summed up by placing them in three general categories. We have seen examples of gross mismanagement, of poor or bad judgment, and a lack of courage in dealing with Canada's economic problems.
If I may turn to each of these three categories in turn, one example of mismanagement that comes readily to mind has to do with the student summer employment program announced by the government not long ago. I find it very interesting to note the comments of some of the officials who say they feel we are doing reasonably

May 18, 1971
Measures to Improve Economy well in dealing with this situation, considering that the program had been introduced so late in the season. I suggest this is nothing but poor management. The government has been unable to bring forward its announcements and plans until this late date, and this will have a detrimental effect on solving the over-all problems facing the Canadian economy at this time.
Secondly, with respect to poor judgment we have very ready examples of this in the inadequacy of government programs which have been introduced over the past year or two to cope with the series of economic problems that have arisen. I have read in a number of publications, such as The Executive, a magazine certainly not unsympathetic to the federal government, and elsewhere that government officials were astounded that the economy had been so slow in responding to some of the policy initiatives introduced by the government, first of all to deal with the problem of inflation which the government was really rolling up its sleeves to tackle. It took a long time to get any sort of response at all. I read that government officials simply could not understand this and were very surprised that the economy was so slow in responding to the measures taken by the government.
Similarly in dealing with the unemployment problem which has grown rapidly during the past winter, again government officials could not understand, according to some of the publications I have read, why it took so long for the economy to respond to some of the initiatives that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and others were bragging about in this House. I feel this is a case of poor judgment. Somehow the government has lost its grip on and control of the situation. It is not able to handle it any longer, so it flounders about from crisis to crisis. In addition we have seen a demonstrated lack of courage in tackling some of the problems that exist.
To analyse the situation I think we must look at what is happening to the Canadian economy today. Why have government officials been so surprised? Why has the government found it difficult to understand why the economy has been so slow to respond to policy initiatives? I think the answer is very simple: the Canadian economy has changed. It is a different sort of economy today from what it was a number of years ago. Today we have a managed economy, not an economy managed by the government or an economy that is operating in a free market but one that for the most part is controlled by large corporations which call the tune, which take the initiatives that determine the course of affairs in the Canadian economy. I have seen it demonstrated by this government that it is not willing to tackle the sources of economic power in Canada, or the seat of economy power in Canada, in order to deal with the economic problems that are plaguing the Canadian nation.
This afternoon I listened to the Minister of Finance taking part in this debate and could not help but feel sorry for him. I thought back to last Thursday and his statements about the unemployment figures that were announced. He simply could not understand what was the trouble, what was causing the increase or why it was that government policies had not been more effective. He
was floundering about in helpless fashion. We had a further example this afternoon when the minister was pretty hard put to try to come up with any sort of plausible defence of government policy.
It seems to me that there is a noticeable lack of enthusiasm and support for the minister and his policies from the government benches. This is demonstrated by the absence of participation in this debate by government members. Since the Minister of Finance spoke, I understand that one other government member has made a speech in the debate, which is one more indicator to me that there is a very noticeable lack of enthusiasm for the policies of the minister and for the situation in which he finds himself. In response to the speech made by my colleague from Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) the minister tried to say that many countries would like to have an economy with the record that Canada's has. I question that statement very much. Many countries are doing as well as or better than Canada, and with a good deal less in the way of resources at their disposal.
I note that the minister also disagreed with my colleague in his references to the need to put the resource industries of Canada-the primary resource industries, the minerals industry, and so on-on the same footing as the rest of the Canadian economy and to take away the special advantages that they enjoy today. The minister has the right to disagree. In fact, in doing so he is being consistent because this is in line with the statements he has made over the past several months in which he made it very clear that the tax concessions which these industries have enjoyed for so many years will be continued for a further period.
I also noted that the Minister of Finance did acknowledge that there were some problems. I believe he referred to them as trouble spots in Canada. It seems to me a rather euphemistic expression, to refer to the 659,000 people in Canada who were out of work during the month of April as simply being trouble spots. That is a great many trouble spots! I suggest it is time the Minister of Finance woke up and realized the situation.
He also attempted to analyse the unemployment situation. If I interpreted him correctly, he gave the impression there are problems but things are going all right; there are some good indicators in the Canadian economy which show that things are on the upward trend. This does not do away with the fact that there are still 659,000 people out of work.
I was also amazed to note that the Minister of Finance was so hard up to find a defence for his policies and, in some cases, the lack of them, that he had to start worrying about the recent NDP federal convention. I suggest he will have to worry a great deal more about the NDP and its federal convention than he has up to the present time. I assure him, just to set his mind at rest, that there is absolutely no problem of reconciliation between NDP policy as set down at that convention and past conventions and the position being taken by NDP members of the House of Commons.

May 18, 1971

The Minister of Finance did acknowledge that there were some problems concerning unemployment, and that unemployment was at a level which made all of us unhappy. I should not expect any less from the minister in that regard. It seems to me he must take a closer look at what is happening to the Canadian economy at the present time. The fact is that in April, 1971, there were
342.000	people in Canada who had been out of work for four months or longer. That compares with 308,000 people in the same category in March, 1971, and only
229.000 in the same category in April of 1970.
Attention has also been drawn to the large number of
young people who are out of work at the present time. This is a source of serious concern in Canada. I also find that there has been an increase in unemployment at every age level set out by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. I noticed that the minister was so hard pressed to deal with the problem that he had to blame it on the winter. I acknowledge there have been problems in some parts of Canada in that regard which would have a temporary effect and which may be overcome in another month. I also know that in every region across Canada, except in the parts furthest west, there was a notable increase in unemployment in the month of April as compared with March.
In the Atlantic region, unemployment for April was 11.6 per cent, compared with 10.9 per cent in the month of March. I have not been in the Atlantic provinces recently, but the information I have does not suggest that their winter or spring conditions were so bad they could account for the increase in unemployment that took place between March and April. It seems to me a much closer analysis is required of the situation than the Minister of Finance has come forward with up to the present time.
I should like to briefly refer to three areas which I think deserve special attention in attempting to deal with Canada's serious economic situation. The first area concerns the problems of rural Canada. This is having a very serious effect on the Canadian economy. Farm income in Canada in 1970 was $1,198 million, which is 23.9 per cent less than the 1969 level of $1,595 million. This is bound to have a serious effect on the Canadian economy and on employment in centres such as Brantford where a large part of the farm machinery manufacturing industry is located.
In my own province of Saskatchewan, the farm net income in 1970 was $202 million. This is $200 million less than the $402 million for 1969. In 1970 the net income level for farmers in Saskatchewan was cut in half. We see the results of what is happening in the drift away from farms into the cities of people who do not have skills with which they can demand a decent and adequate level of income. We also see what is happening to our rural communities and small urban centres, those complexes involved with the rural community structure. We have made proposals for emergency assistance on a long-term basis which would help to deal with these problems by increasing the net income available to farmers and our rural people. These would be much more beneficial than the proposals which have been brought forward by the government.
Measures to Improve Economy
Secondly, I suggest the government's policy dealing with regional development has been an unmitigated disaster. The minister sloughs off criticism, but he is not able to come up with any concrete answers. He simply says we are doing all right, we are giving away millions of dollars in grants, much of it to large corporations which have no need of it. There are no plans available to deal with the economic problems of the underdeveloped regions of Canada or regions which do not come up to the average of Canadian income.
I suggest, thirdly, there is a need for reorientation of our trade policy. I noticed the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) was bragging this afternoon about our export surplus when answering a question during the question period. On the other hand, the Minister of Finance was expressing concern and worry about the export surplus. This shows that the government is having a good deal of difficulty co-ordinating its position. We must find out what our trade policy is. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce always answers by saying we must keep a balance.
What is the government doing to take into account the growth of new trade complexes, particularly the European Common Market? How are we going to adjust to this, and what is the government's response? The minister says we are going to undertake multilateral negotiations to reduce tariffs and other non-tariff trade barriers in Canada. We have to come up with alternatives. Canada must consider what it will do if such multilateral negotiations are not successful or are not possible. We have yet to hear from the government what its answers are. I commend the motion moved by my colleague the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman).

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR ECONOMIC MEASURES, PLANNED INVESTMENT AND FOREIGN OWNERSHIP POLICIES TO ACHIEVE HIGH EMPLOYMENT THROUGH DEVELOPMENT OF SECONDARY MANUFACTURING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I cannot support this motion put forward by the hon. member of the NDP, I think it is a good idea in one sense to have a debate at this time on the economic status of the country. I say this for three reasons. This country is experiencing, and in all likelihood will continue to experience, levels of unemployment without economic or humane justification. It has become manifestly apparent that the government's attempts to curb inflation have not been successful in that they have not had any effect in reducing unemployment.
Finally, the government has allowed the Canadian dollar to reach a level in international monetary markets which, by the Prime Minister's own admission recently in Vancouver, is harming our international trade upon which our economy is vitally dependent. This can be related particularly to the economy of the western grains industry which last year lost $90 million to $100 million as a result of the increased value of the dollar.
The government has suffered the embarrassment of having two of its most articulate ministers resign from the cabinet over its economic policies. In more normal times one would be content to view such resignations as a somewhat unavoidable result of the interplay of strong personalities. However, when one examines the figures of the labour force contained in the press release for the week ending April 17, he finds that the unadjusted rate

May 18, 1971
Measures to Improve Economy of unemployment is 7.8 per cent. When one also remembers that the increase in unemployment is the largest in 13 years, one begins to understand some of the true and bitter realities of the current state of our economy.
It cannot but be cause for the most serious concern by each of us in the House when we remember that the unemployment figures to which I have referred do not include the effect on the Canadian labour force of the several hundred thousand young people who will be leaving our secondary schools, technical colleges and universities to seek either permanent or temporary employment. Let us also remember that at about this time of year a very large percentage of the people undergoing training courses sponsored by the Department of Manpower and Immigration will be coming onto the labour market.
Notwithstanding the infinitely broader and perhaps even more fundamental question of the effects of automation on the concept of full employment in a highly industrialized and specialized society such as we have, we must remember that not only is the work ethic still dominant in Canada but more important is the fact that work is a basic necessity for the individual's well-being as well as that of the nation collectively. In our society one is defined largely in terms of what he does to earn his living. I do not suggest that this is a correct concept, but it is an inescapable fact. Thus, when one is deprived of the opportunity to earn his living he becomes deprived of much of his personal sense of worth.
The sociological and psychological effects of mass unemployment, particularly amongst our young, well educated people, our skilled tradesmen and technicians, is an evil which must be rooted out of our society before it leads to the most destructive consequences. No longer are our people prepared to accept such conditions as inevitable features of a free enterprise economy. If the government cannot find the solution to the malignancy of massive unemployment, I have not the slightest doubt that the radical forces in this country will be joined by a great many of our younger citizens who Eire, understandably, disillusioned with the inability of the government, with all its massive resources, to lead this country in a manner which enables those who are capable and desirous of working to find appropriate employment.
Mr. Speaker, it is all very well for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to say that he accepts the responsibility for unemployment, but I ask: What are the practical effects of such a declaration? Does it in any significant way ease the soul-destroying anguish of the unemployed father whose insurance benefits have expired and who, still being unable to find employment because of the government's economic policies, must now resort to the indignity of seeking welfare to sustain his family? I can assure you that the Prime Minister's words are of no comfort whatever.
There is an old cliche which states that poverty is not a disgrace. I say that in this country, in this day and age, poverty brought about in large measure by the government's deliberate policies is not only a disgrace but a moral condemnation of our whole society. We are not without control over our economic destiny and when the government embarks on certain courses of action it is because it has chosen them over others. The policies which the present government has pursued in attempting to manage the economy reflect the most insensitive aspects of nineteenth century economic thinking.
One can only hope that on some glorious day in the next few weeks, possibly on the occasion of the presentation of the budget to this House next month, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and his chief advisers will be dragged into the twentieth century, notwithstanding the resistance which they will obviously offer to the pursuit of policies which reflect and serve the needs of the average Canadian as opposed to satisfying the view of the government's economic advisers whose advice, presuming it has been accepted, has so disastrously affected our country.
Mr. Speaker, figures recently released by the government indicate that its battle against inflation could well result in its being routed out of office by a justifiably angered population. The trend in the first quarter of this year indicates that if inflation continues to grow at its present rate we shall have nearly 6 per cent inflation for the whole year. Once again, people on fixed incomes or modest pensions, who are supposed to be the beneficiaries of the government's anti-inflationary policies, will be the most cruelly affected. We must also consider the effect of this renewed round of inflationary pressures on interest rates generally in our economy.
In the Globe and Mail of today I noted in the financial section an article entitled "Interest rate rise looms". The article dealt in general terms with the effect on interest rates in the United States of the current international monetary difficulties in Europe, as well as the general reappearance of inflationary factors in the economy. I should like to quote one paragraph from that article because of its relevance to Canada. It reads:
An indication of the kind of problems posed to potential borrowers by today's capital market conditions is Quebec's continuing hesitation over its planned 100 million dollars (United States) issue in New York. Postponed once because of market uncertainties, this is currently scheduled for early next week. But the province's financial managers remain very concerned about disturbed market conditions, and it would not be at all surprising if the issue were postponed again.
Mr. Speaker, when borrowers become apprehensive about borrowing because of existing interest rates, or provisions in their borrowing contracts to provide for adjustments according to market fluctuations, or when lenders refuse to do so unless borrowers agree to escalator clauses in the borrowing market, then the market reaches a situation which prohibits growth because the capital investment on which our economy is so dependent becomes simply too speculative and risky for either the borrower or the lender.
When mortgage rates-I Eim speaking of prime mortgages-command interest rates of 10 per cent and 11 per cent as they have in recent months, and when businessmen must pay similar rates or even higher in order to

borrow money needed for their day to day operations, one sees just how blatantly ineffective the government's so-called anti-inflationary policies have been. What disturbs me is that our chartered banks, trust and insurance companies and other major lenders having tasted the sweet blood of double-figured interest rates will not be content to have interest rates return to sensible levels. Mr. Speaker, I shall leave that point and pass on to my last point of disagreement with the government's management of our economy, which involves the unpegging of the Canadian dollar. At a time when Canadian industry has been experiencing inflation at home increasingly strong competition from other countries for its world markets and excessive demands by some parts of the economy, the government has for some mysterious reason seen fit to aggravate their difficulties by unpegging our dollar and allowing it to rise to parity with the United States dollar. In fairness I must say that the Minister of Finance and the government have been consistent in refusing to alter the decision once it had been made. No matter how harmful or manifestly wrong it is shown to be for Canada, they will nevertheless continue to cling to it.
Mr. Speaker, in the Montreal Gazette of May 6, 1971, there appeared an article by that paper's financial columnist, Mr. John Meyer, entitled "And what if our dollar had been repegged?". It reads:
Finance Minister Benson has refused to be rushed into repegging the Canadian dollar. The wisdom of that course should now be readily apparent in the difficulties being experienced by West Germany and, to a lesser degree, Holland, Belgium, Austria and Switzerland. The deutschemark has been formally set afloat and the currencies of the other countries are floating in fact, if not yet formally proclaimed to be doing so.
Measures to Improve Economy
Had the Canadian dollar been repegged, it too would be under the sort of pressure being felt in Europe and which, in the long run, courts national bankruptcy to attempt to resist indefinitely.
Finally, he says:
It's extremely doubtful that the United States feels any serious compulsion to go beyond the current adjustments in its policies. Why should it? It's the principal beneficiary of any upward revaluation, relative to the U.S. dollar, or the deutschemark or any other currency, including the Canadian dollar. The higher the foreign currency, the less competitive are imports, the more competitive American exports ...
What is being demonstrated here is the extent to which, in a context of fixed currency relationships, the policies adopted in the United States can influence those of its trading partners. When those policies are taken to extremes, as they have been the past two years, they can cause similarly extreme reactions abroad until relief is obtained by breaking away from a fixed relationship.
I think it is time for the Canadian government to look at the repegging of the Canadian dollar, even if it is done in the so-called narrow range, with a crawling peg or by some other mechanism. I think our exports will be hurt badly if we do not look very closely at the value of the Canadian dollar.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would have been willing to listen to the rest of the minister's statement which would have taken only a few moments. From this statement we can however guess how he feels about his government's administration.
Of course I would have been quite surprised if the minister had condemned his government's policy. I do not think the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) would have had the nerve of the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer), for instance, or of the former Minister of Communications (Mr. Kierans) who have both severely condemned this government's economic policy.
The contribution of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to this debate is rather insignificant, because we already knew that he was going to commend the approach of this party and of the cabinet, of which he is a member.
However, the people who might read his remarks as well as those of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) will completely disagree with both of them.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate and thank the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) for having introduced this motion this afternoon. It puts forward a number of quite acceptable principles. However, its success will depend on the performance of those called upon to apply them and to establish, as requested, special programs designed to move the economy to high employment.
In fact, the Liberal party tried to achieve such objectives, but, it seems to me, in a somewhat abnormal fashion. It proceeded from bottom to top, whereas it should have done the opposite.
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand), with his subsidies program, also tried to bring about a high level of employment, but with a view to solving the production problems. He attempted to settle non-existent problems, for there are no production problems in Canada at the present time. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce has just said that he does his best to increase our export trade because we have too many products.
A war is now being waged among the provinces, because of a glut rather than a scarcity of products. The provincial authorities are now erecting walls between the provinces to prevent interprovincial trade.
Not so long ago, I heard the premier of Saskatchewan, Mr. Ross Thatcher, say that the main problem now is overproduction.
At a time when we find overproduction everywhere, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion generously subsidizes the industries in order to help them produce more. All those amounts that are given out do not reach
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Richard).]
the consumers because the problem does not exist at the production level but at the consumer level. That is where the real problem is.
Instead of subsidizing production, the minister and the government should have subsidized the consumers. Thus, consumers, particularly those who are in need-whether they are unemployed, handicapped people or older people-could have benefited from the production at their disposal and through consumer subsidies they could have ordered from producers and industrialists the kind of production they want.
But the opposite is the case at the present time; producers are subsidized and there are some who would like consumers to buy the goods that are made for them. But as the system in which we live is increasingly automated, those subsidies given out to the industry are not always profitable to workers but they are profitable to the machines that replace them.
I just read a report stating that some steelworks had been constructed in Japan recently where not a single worker is needed for the production of parts. One is needed at the door to direct the iron towards the works and, when the process is completed, another is required to ship the product.
The same situation can be found fairly often in a large number of industries, and we are told that in the near future a similar process will be used everywhere.
When industry is subsidized, it is fairly often the purchase of machinery to replace the workers that is subsidized. Consumers do not benefit from such subsidies and yet those are paid with their taxes.
The motion submitted by the hon. member for Waterloo states, in part:
.-emergency economic measures to move the economy to high employment-
That is a change in the New Democratic Party's use of terms. Not so long ago, full employment was what we spoke of; now, we speak of a high level of employment because, when you give the matter some thought, it is increasingly difficult to achieve, full employment what with machinery, automation, cybernetics even.
The motion also calls for:
-expansionary monetary and fiscal policies
But no ways and means are indicated. There are means of extending the monetary field, but care must be exercised. It must indeed be noted that over the past 10, 20, 30 years, there has been a monetary expansion, but this has been achieved through debts. We are still paying interest on debts contracted 30 or 40 years ago. Such a monetary expansion is not favourable to the development of Canada, or to an improvement in the Canadian standard of living.
Expansion in the fiscal area is also advocated. That worries me because I have learned from experience in public affairs that every move toward fiscal expansion has always been to increase taxes. The only fiscal
May 18, 1971

changes that have been made have been tax increases. Therefore, this request worries me a lot.
The government is also called upon
-to achieve full potential growth through a planned investment and foreign ownership policy-
Mr. Speaker, I think this is acceptable with regard to local investments, but we must be careful about foreign capital. Indeed, we have seen the premiers of nearly all Canadian provinces go around the world in order to get foreign capital. But each time we succeeded in getting foreign countries interested in investing capital here, we paid for it. Each year, we must let profits go out of the country back to those investors. The fact that those sums or benefits go back to their foreign sources means that we are deprived of that much in capital assets.
So, Mr. Speaker, I think that local investment should be promoted to a much greater extent than foreign investment. But how is that going to be achieved?
It happens, Mr. Speaker, that in private industry or in business we lack funds. Savings accumulate here and there, but they are attracted by high interest rates offered by the federal, provincial and particularly municipal governments. The three levels of government are at war to attract the savings of individuals, because in the first place a rather high interest is paid, and also because garantees are offered on bond issues sold to the public. Thus all those savings are drained off by the public enterprise and none are left for private enterprises.
The Social Credit advocates the following solution. The government, through the Bank of Canada, should make funds available to non-profit public corporations which render some services to the Canadian people. Thus, individual savings would be available to private enterprise. We could then refer to local investments, because there would be some capital to invest.
Those are the few considerations which I wanted to state during my contribution to this debate on the motion under consideration.
The motion concludes with a request that a stimulus be provided for the development of secondary manufacturing. Well, Mr. Speaker, this request should have been complied with a long time ago.
There is a serious lack of secondary industries in Canada. We are still only extracting natural resources that we are mostly shipping as raw materials.
A few moments ago, I was referring to the case of a new highly automated Japanese steel mill. I did not say that this was the first one. In fact, there are many others and we sire aware that Japan is a big importer of iron, coal and copper from Canada, but they import these as raw materials, to be refined and processed.
I think that in such a field, Canada would find it profitable to facilitate the establishment of industries to promote the creation of secondary industries, in order to process our raw materials here.
Our country, particularly the northern area, abounds in ores of various kinds and we are satisfied with burying our miners underground to extract the ore, ship it to foreign countries where it is refined and then shipped
Measures to Improve Economy back to us for our own use. There is no rhyme or reason to this, and immediate steps should be taken to change this situation.
Thanks to our labour, equipment and technology we could be much more self-sufficient than we are today, and it would be to our advantage.
Those are the few considerations which I wanted to express tonight in connection with the motion before the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was rather refreshing to hear the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin). He talked about the problems of the secondary industry, and unemployment. I thought back to 1962. At that time we pegged the dollar in order to permit our secondary industries and primary producers to compete in the world and regain full employment. At that time some hon. members, including some who are still here and the former Secretary of State for External Affairs who has gone to the other place, wandered up and down the land and brought our government to a minority position. Today the problem is that the government has freed the dollar and we have priced ourselves out of world-markets, no matter how you dish it out. That is the ironic part about politics.
The government does not now, and never has had, a comprehensive, realistic policy on foreign investment. We have heard a lot about it. At best, the government has instituted a series of ad hoc arrangements which mean that it is responding to one crisis after another. It is known as a crisis government. The government has substituted brinkmanship for sound, rational investment policy. The results for Canada have been catastrophic. As a result, we have high unemployment together with inflation, although the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said he had inflation licked. Inflation has licked the Prime Minister, and unemployment is going to lick this government.
The Canadian government's decision to save Home Oil for Canadian investors stands in glaring counter-distinction to this and the Quebec governments' intention to finance the James Bay project with foreign, mainly United States, capital to the tune of $2 billion, regardless of its effect on the ecology. So once again western Canada is discriminated against. Although Home Oil is one of the biggest independent companies in Canada, the government has said no, it cannot be sold to foreign investors. But it is fine if Quebec, through this government, brings in $2 billion of foreign investment to take over the resources of that province, when the province of Quebec-I hope Quebeckers will hear my voice through the media-has one of the highest unemployment rates in Canada. We are going to give away electrical energy. We are using United States capital to finance Quebec's resources and to give Americans jobs that the workers in the province of Quebec should have.
