speechtext:
If you will just listen I will tell you what can be done about it. This government has shown a glaring inability to do anything about it. There are certain facts that would constrain a rational approach by the government in the field of foreign investment. With respect to our foreign investment policy as it is applied to natural resource development, it is obvious that the federal government cannot have such a policy unless that policy intimately and meaningfully implicates the provincial governments. The reason for this is simple. It is the constitutional prerogative of the provinces to develop their own natural resources.
We all know what happened at the time of the Bennett government when the natural resources of western Canada were returned to the provinces. The federal government has only a limited role to play in this area. I agree that is the case, but it has to be worked out with the provinces. However, this limited role can be an important one if the federal government and the provinces can agree to certain guidelines relating to foreign investment and natural resource development. Such guidelines will always be impossible to achieve if the federal government persists in operating an economy wherein provincial governments find it difficult, if not impossible, to attain their own economic objectives. The reason Bourassa and the Quebec Liberal government has decided not to wait for Ottawa is that they, like Ontario and Alberta, are convinced that the federal government's economic policies are not in the best interests of Canada as a whole or any individual province.
The important thing to underline in any discussion concerning intergovernmental co-operation is the need for the federal government to pledge that it will do everything in its power to ensure that Canada fully utilizes all of its economic potential. A full employment, growth-oriented, dynamic economy ensures that Canada will gain economic degrees of freedom to pursue an independent, rational investment policy regarding our natural resources. The reason the Quebec government is not waiting for the federal government is that Quebec is convinced that the federal government's economic policies are not in Quebec's own interests; and neither are they in the interests of western Canada.
If Ottawa is not providing the economic climate which is conducive to Quebec's growth, then Quebec will go outside Canada to get the moneys available to develop Quebec, as it has had to do, at the same time handing over its jobs to United States workers. In the same sort of way, Ontario is not prepared to stand still while Ottawa screws up the Canadian economy. Intergovernmental co-operation on economic matters is impossible so long as the provinces are convinced that Ottawa's economics are not in their own best interests. This government will not even discuss a problem so important to the welfare of all Canadians at a constitutional conference.
We were asked what we would do when we formed the government. After establishing a full employment, economic policy.-and we on this side of the House have made it clear to the government, through my leader, on many occasions how we would get the economy moving again at full strength-we would have to tackle in a
meaningful way the problem of foreign investment. I do not have much time to go into detail, but these are some of the actions that we would consider taking. First of all, we need proper information. There is a lot of false information concerning foreign investment, for political reasons. What we need is proper information about the actions of foreign subsidiaries in Canada. Without information there can be no clear understanding of what these subsidiaries are doing and what Canada might want them to do differently. Increased financial disclosure by private companies is necessary in order to come to a decision; I think everybody would agree with that.
Secondly, having obtained proper information we would need to decide in which sectors of the Canadian economy foreign investment should be restricted or regulated. If we pulled out foreign investment in Canada tomorrow, it would be like pulling the plug out of a big bathtub; we would just hear the water gurgling, and further unemployment would be the result. We must consider, first, the importance of the sector to economic planning. By economic planning I mean devising appropriate rules and regulations and establishing the proper economic climate. Then we must consider the policy-leverage aspects of the sector, that is, the importance of the sector in allowing the government's economic policies to become more effective.
Then we must consider, if we are going to be nationalistic at all, the cultural sensitivity of the sector, that is, its importance as a factor in the establishment and maintenance of a Canadian identity. We have to ask ourselves the question: Do we want to remain Canadian?
Thirdly, the key sector concept raises two questions. Is there adequate Canadian capital and entrepreneurship to man these sectors? It is no good our saying that there is enough capital in Canada to build a pipe line from the Arctic down through the Mackenzie Valley to the midwest. As a matter of fact, it would be a shorter distance to transport natural gas or crude petroleum from King Christian Island to eastern Canada were the pipe line is. It is 1,500 miles closer than the Mackenzie Valley route. Yet I question whether the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) even knows this. He has no policy-only the kind of breeze that he blows from time to time-and speaks without knowledge, as he showed us the other day when he made his statement.
The second question we should ask ourselves is, how one can be sure that Canadian-controlled enterprises will behave in a way that coincides more closely with Canadian national interests? It is frequently claimed that sufficient Canadian savings exist to provide for Canadian-owned investments in the full amount needed for the development of our country. The argument is that foreign subsidiaries have been expanding 85 per cent through the use of retained earnings generated in Canada and only 15 per cent through the use of the inflow of new capital. In these terms the adequacy of savings begs the question whether these savings would have been generated without the original foreign initiative, and the question regarding the right and advisability of Canadians to expropriate these savings for their own use.

May 18, 1971

When we save money in the bank, our savings are invested in various ways. But there is a need for foreign capital. My point is: How do you determine just where it should be used, and in what sector, so as to create a climate in which the economy can be kept moving, at the same time retaining some form of Canadian stamp or control?
A more relevant proposal is the provision of further incentives to holders of Canadian institutionalized savings-that is, mutual funds, pension funds and insurance funds-to invest in Canadian enterprises. At the extreme, these incentives might be made a requirement. The stimulation of Canadian entrepreneurship is a far more difficult question since it is by no means easy to locate it and to quantify its potential.
A proposal in this area must provide for two phases, one short-run and another long-run. In the short run it is necessary to provide financial incentives and assistance to the operation of new firms in key sectors, including assistance with the importation of technology and the arrangement of management contracts. In the long run it is necessary to produce greater numbers of entrepreneurs and people with the kind of managerial skills that we need. Representatives of business and of schools of administration should be encouraged to research this question and, where possible, to adjust their programs to provide more extensive and appropriate learning experiences.
The claim for Canadian equity participation in Canadian firms, either minority, majority or controlling, is not a claim that the view of Canadian corporate owners will necessarily coincide with that of Canadian governments; there will be some confrontations. Rather, it is based on the view that Canadian owners and managers will be more receptive to and have a better appreciation of the reasons underlying Canadian government policies than will foreign owners and managers. We have to be shown that. It has to be proven.
A number of proposals are made which will help sensitize foreign-owned firms in Canada to Canadian government policy. First, federally-incorporated companies should be required to have at least three Canadian citizens as members of the Canadian board of directors, at least two of whom should be outsiders who are not connected with the company. This would ensure exposure of the board to Canadian opinion and view. At the same time they should show a fair profit and return.
In order to sensitize foreign subsidiaries to Canadian conditions, the Canadian directors should be provided with lists of their duties as directors, for which they should be held legally responsible. This should be the case in respect of the companies acts of the provincial governments or the federal government. The board of directors should be held responsible for its decisions. This proposal is an attempt to prevent the appointment of Canadian directors becoming a rubber-stamp operation and it is a recognition of the need for the Canadian government to state more precisely what is expected
Measures to Improve Economy
from foreign subsidiaries. The United States does this, and Canada can do it. I do not think anyone would think for one moment that the United States would not continue to invest in this country provided there was the kind of confidence in Canada that there should be. One of the reasons the United States is investing today in Germany and Japan is that it has lost confidence in Canada, and I put the onus for this on the government.
A policy toward foreign takeovers should be developed in line with the establishment of key sectors. Foreign takeovers of Canadian firms in key sectors should be monitored and restricted, although not necessarily disallowed. A takeover in a key sector might be permitted where there was a commitment to make equity available to Canadians over a number of years. When the stock was issued for the Alberta gas line, which was controlled, engineered and initiated by the provincial government, every citizen of Alberta had the opportunity to invest up to $20 in the stock of that company.

With regard to promoting secondary industry, about which we have spoken on this side, the minister mentioned the methods being used to accomplish this end. In the few minutes at my disposal I should like to deal with an issue which will come before this House and the country in the very near future. I would say it is. I think members opposite will And that a great many Liberals throughout the country, not only in this House, are inclined to accept the record, and it is quite evident. It has been expounded in the last year or so that restrictive measures do not work. Indeed, expansionist measures and the adoption of the ideas of some of our new economists such as Miss Diane Cohen, Mr. Weldon and Mr. Friedman, will have a great bearing on the policies of this government. Therefore, I think the motion is quite good.
Let me say to members opposite who proposed this motion that one of the essentials to a successful conclusion is this: If we are indeed going to adopt expansionist measures, we will have to bring our economy and our industry into greater efficiency. We will be faced with this problem in the forthcoming budget. If we are to keep inflation under control we must be very selective in making tax concessions. There is an argument at the present time that if we allow tax concessions across the board there will be an inflationary push. The hon. gentleman opposite shakes his head, but I suggest there will be an inflationary push.
If there is already a push and a squeeze between manufacturers' costs and the sales position, and you throw $500 mihion or $600 million into the consumers' hands, there will be immediately an upward price movement. If this will mean an inflationary push, we must think of another method. We must give tax concessions to corporations and businesses: it is their reserves which are decimated. They cannot get loans to buy new equipment and machinery because the banks know they have a poor profit picture and that their reserves are down to nil.
If we gave tax concessions to the corporations they would have to make a profit by selling their goods at a low price. If we did this, just think what hon. members across the way might say. Everyone over there would rise with indignation and ask what we had done. They would suggest we had given tax concessions to business and nothing to the poor consumers.

speechtext:
Just what we intended to do. I ask the hon. gentleman opposite how new policies can be adopted when they are ingrained with the old policies. What gentlemen opposite are saying is that we should adopt new concepts and new expansionist policies, but do not show any favouritism toward business-give the concessions to the consumer. This is the position they take in the motion. The last part of the motion refers specifically to the fact that the people who will succeed in getting other people to work are the entrepreneurs. We have to come to this conclusion in some way.
With regard to secondary industry, I should like to direct the attention of the House to the most recent United States labour figures. It is surprising to find that 63 per cent of American people are employed in the service industries. That covers everything from superintendent of a plant to a salesman, the sales manager, the executive, junior executives, lawyers, architects and engineers. Only 37 per cent are employed in the factories operating machines and producing goods. There is already an impetus for a large number of Canadians to work in factories producing goods. In a short time we will not be saying we are the hewers of wood and the drawers of water; we will be complaining we are the ones making the goods by working in the factories and the Americans are the ones who occupy the high positions in industry. There is already a movement in that direction and I think it will continue for the next 10 or 15 years. We are already considering the next phase, which is foreign ownership. I will deal with that matter in a minute.
Mr. Speaker, this government should recognize that if we are to have any influence over secondary industry we must re-think two positions we have adopted over the last five years. I believe hon. gentlemen on this side of the House have already brought this matter to the attention of the government. If we continue our regional incentive programs it is completely incongruous to say we will promote industry in those regions where industry really is not suited, and at the same time try to bring more efficiency into our economy. This is impossible, because what we are really saying in all our regional incentive programs is that the government will pay from $2,500 to possibly $10,000 per job for an industry to establish itself in an area, which economically does not make sense. This only deprives other, more efficient areas of this type of industry.
So we are at cross-purposes. We may decide to put an industry in northern Ontario or northern Quebec a long way from the market and in an area where there are transportation and technological problems. We say we will pay an industry to go there, and at the same time complain that the industry is not efficient. Of course it is not efficient because it is competing with the Germans and Japanese who are very sophisticated.
While speaking of the German market, we must consider their position in respect of free enterprise and anti-combines legislation. In the last two years, hon. members will be interested to know, the German coal industry found itself in a serious predicament. The industry was competitive; it had about 57 plants and 103 enterprises, none of which was making money. As a result, two years ago the German government sponsored and promoted a combine, the Ruhr Coal A.G. This is a company which now controls all the German coal producers. It is working toward an efficient combine and monopoly in order to make the German coal industry prosper, while we on the other hand have not acknowledged that there is a time when we must re-think our

May 18, 1971

ideas in respect of industries in which an element of competition no longer applies.
In some industries there is no competition. There are large corporations which probably tolerate a smaller competitor merely as a figurehead. The fact is, however, that a certain segment of our industrial enterprise has no competition. We should accept that fact and promote some sort of combine or monopoly to make it more efficient, rather than have each enterprise lose money.
This brings me to the question of foreign control. I believe the policy the government will introduce on this issue will be found to be acceptable and welcome to the whole country. But I have never worried too much about control in respect of Canadian industry. The real issue is efficiency. There is a second and possibly just as important consideration. We as Canadians must decide which industries are to be exploited and promoted, although not on a worldwide basis because we are not concerned about a multinational corporation as an investment in Tanganyika or Brazil even though it would be more profitable to establish it there than in New Brunswick or Ontario. We must consider it from the Canadian point of view.
After more than 22 years in business I have learned that there is no school, university or educational process within which to train executive cadre, other than apprenticeship. It is an unfortunate fact in multinational corporations that when it comes to the man who makes the decisions, someone is always sent here to manage. So we have nowhere in which to exercise apprenticeship. Therefore, the United States executive is much more efficient. We should have a policy which would allow our young people to enter the executive cadre and assume control of corporations. We should regulate this matter.
There is another element which possibly has never been emphasized. The United States industrial enterprise is very great and has a vast accumulation of capital. Our presumption always has been that capital comes from savings. I deny this. Venture capital, or risk capital, does not come from the money we accumulate by scrimping and saving. This money is used to buy insurance policies, something nice and safe. The money which is invested and reinvested is the money which comes from dividends. If we look at the record of dividend payments and reinvestment of dividends we will find that a fantastic proportion of the dividends received by a shareholder are put back into the market. We do not have this.
The United States has the world's largest reserves of capital investment. So, as an hon. member said, it is important to ensure that eventually Canadians will be able to buy this equity and obtain shares in order to reinvest the money. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I strongly supported the white paper on tax reform because it emphasized the need to provide a wider distribution of shares in the country.
I do not think any of us would find anything to argue about in this motion. It is a question of timing and a question of emphasis. So far as this motion is concerned, the government has done more than it asks for. Indeed, there is nothing in the motion that we have not done or
Measures to Improve Economy
are not in the process of doing. Therefore I do not find any difficulty in supporting it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR ECONOMIC MEASURES, PLANNED INVESTMENT AND FOREIGN OWNERSHIP POLICIES TO ACHIEVE HIGH EMPLOYMENT THROUGH DEVELOPMENT OF SECONDARY MANUFACTURING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the remarks of the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto). Having heard them, I only wish that this influence on the policies of the government was a bit more profound. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) during his remarks charged the opposition with being somewhat intemperate in its attack, and with failing to realize that the circumstances in which this country's economy now finds itself are at worst the honest mistakes of honest men attempting to do an honest job in the very imprecise area of economics. We are all aware of this. What makes us intemperate, if such we are, is the distorted value system upon which this government has based its policies.
Perhaps I might illustrate what I mean. This afternoon I listened with absolute horror and total disbelief to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howard, Okanagan Boundary) defend his government's economic policies. In commenting on those remarks I will be employing language which does not come easily to my tongue. However, I make no apology for this because the kind of social philosophy presented to us by the parliamentary secretary can only be described as disgusting by any civilized group of men.
He told us that we could have full employment if we were willing to sacrifice our standard of living. He implied that we would not be willing to make such a sacrifice. For the moment I will leave aside the validity or lack of validity of the direct relationship he implied between high rates of employment and low standards of living. I want to emphasize that a member of the government stood in his place and told us, in effect, that if forced to choose between 600,000 or 700,000 men and women being stripped of their dignity through being denied gainful employment and having to give up the opportunity for some of the niceties of life available to the fortunate third of the people in North America, he would choose the second television set. I thought that today one could only find people with that total absence of social conscience in the works of Charles Dickens.
What an utterly barren, hopelessly antique, totally depraved approach for man to say, "I will fight unemployment only if it does not hurt me. I'm all right, Jack"! Moreover, the direct relationship between the standard of living and the rate of unemployment which the parliamentary secretary postulated simply does not exist. He told us of a secretary who went to work in the full employment economy of Germany and had her wages cut in half. He told us of "three mat" apartments in Tokyo and implied that if we in Canada were to achieve full employment, not only would the parliamentary secretary's friends be forced to sell their second Skidoo but all of us would be forced to live like rats in a hole. What a piece of sophistry! What a fatuous bit of histrionics hoping to pass as argument!
No one can deny that the standard of living in the full employment economies of Germany and Japan are below

May 18, 1971
Measures to Improve Economy our own. What the parliamentary secretary neglected to tell us was that the standard of living in those two countries is rapidly overtaking our own. What he neglected to tell us was that the standard of living in the full employment economy of Sweden has already surpassed our own.
Then the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce went on to assert that he had heard no new ideas from the opposition, implying that because they were not new they were valueless. If it does not glitter with new paint, it is no good, whether or not it has been tried. There speaks the petty bourgeois Philistine of nineteenth century literature. He said that even with four ears he would not have heard anything of value from this side of the House today. I would suggest to the hon. member that there must be something between the ears before one can attempt to weigh values.
Enough said about the remarks of the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary. The fact remains that this winter the government had to acknowledge the existence of almost three-quarters of a million unemployed people in Canada. In April, the figure was 659,000, up 9,000 from March. Probably there was and still is further hidden unemployment not measured in the statistics. This situation illustrates vividly the Liberal party's callousness toward people and the total bankruptcy of its economic policies.
Never before in the history of this country did a Prime Minister state before a national audience that it was his government's intention to allow unemployment to rise, if necessary, to 6 per cent to combat inflation. Never before did any federal government knowingly, consciously and with a cool, detached deliberation sentence hundreds of thousands of Canadian workers and their families to the hardships of unemployment. The brutality, the callousness, the studied indifference to the human consequences of this anti-inflationary approach was matched only by its ineptitude. Its ineptitude is measured not only in terms of its social consequences but in terms of its complete failure to deal with the inflationary situation it was supposed to meet. The cost of living figures for the first quarter this year show conclusively that inflation is not licked and that at the same time unemployment is continuing unchecked.
What do the figures in connection with the frightening level of unemployment really mean? We are not talking about statistics; we are talking about hundreds of thousands of human beings. We are not talking only about the unemployed themselves but also about the people who depend upon them and their jobs. These unemployment figures represent human tragedy on a massive scale. They represent fear, want, hopes dashed and confidence undermined. We are not talking about mere figures of 660,000 or 700,000; we are speaking about the immense and continuing suffering, deprivation and spiritual degradation of hundreds of thousands of people as a result of deliberate government policy.
That is why I cannot discuss this subject with any degree of equanimity. Any government that is calculate ingly responsible for such a situation and which speaks
to me about the just society is guilty of total, complete and unparallelled hypocrisy. No government which has looked at the full cost of unemployment would deliberately choose increased unemployment as the answer to inflation. But that is what the Trudeau government has done. New Democrats, in contrast, state that full employment should be the primary economic goal of government. If some price rises occur with full employment or because of shortages or external circumstances, it is far better and cheaper to compensate the victims of inflation, those on fixed incomes, than to squeeze the life out of the economy and pay the staggering bill for unemployment.
In the short run, the present serious shortage of jobs can only be overcome by priming the economy. The New Democratic Party has been urging the government to undertake the following policies immediately. We have urged the institution of a massive public housing program which would be focused on areas of acute shortage and which would involve the provision of additional mortgage money at reasonable interest rates for low-cost housing. We have advocated the stimulation, acceleration and expansion of anti-pollution programs, including capital aid for sewage and waste treatment facilities.
We have advocated the acceleration of other public works projects, but only after re-evaluating their social usefulness. It may be that new post offices might not be nearly as important as new convalescent or nursing-home beds. Making funds available to the provinces and municipalities for such works would be an important feature of the program we are advocating.
Another short-run policy we have advocated in order to supply jobs for the immense number of people out of work is the increasing of purchasing power by tax relief for low-income groups and by increasing allowances to those on pensions and other fixed incomes, together with the inclusion of a cost of living escalator in all such allowances.
We have advocated the tying of new unemployment insurance benefits to the cost of living index, and the extension of seasonal benefits to meet the present emergency. We have also advocated the provision of funds to increase employment opportunities for young people in the area of services to people, such as child care, convalescent services, assistance to elderly persons, recreation, conservation and public health.
To maintain full employment in the long run, this party also advocated a number of policies-among other things, changes in the tax system to end the discrimination in favour of capital-intensive industries. We have advocated an end to the special tax concessions to resource extraction industries which encourage investment in overcapacity there with the result that secondary industries, where the jobs are, lack development capital.
We have advocated an investment reserve system which would involve the placing of a few points of tax on business into a reserve that can be drawn upon within designated periods of time for designated purposes in designated areas. Such a program would make use of the planning capacity of the whole of private industry. We

May 18, 1971

have advocated the creation of a real Canada Development Corporation which would be unequivocally an instrument of government policy and which would be employed to develop secondary industry, to expand resource processing in Canada, to rationalize established industry and to invest in the development of the leading edge of technology.
I could go on into the night listing specific policy suggestions which this party has made. What they all add up to, however, is planning the development of the economy and in so doing ending the haphazard approach to economic development adopted by the present government, policies which the hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans) has aptly described as being "stop-go, boom, bust, rags to riches" and which are at the base of most of our economic ills.
What about controlling inflation? In my opinion, we must begin to face up to the fact that inflation in Canada is largely imported from the United States, largely because of our overdependence upon them as a market and as a supplier to our market and because of the corporate pricing policies of American-owned firms operating in Canada. With these factors operating, even the most draconian measures, such as those the government introduced, can only have a marginal effect, and we have seen that. To end the importing of inflation we must diversify our markets and our suppliers. We must drastically decrease the percentage of our economy which is controlled by foreign-owned corporations. And, finally, we must pray for an end to the war in Viet Nam.
Should we succeed in doing all these things, perhaps fiscal and monetary policies of a normal kind will serve to keep internally-generated inflation at an acceptable level. But the real point is that we must not continue to sacrifice the lives of Canadian men and women on the alter of controlling inflation, a god which in present circumstances cannot be appeased. Instead, we must make full employment our primary economic goal.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR ECONOMIC MEASURES, PLANNED INVESTMENT AND FOREIGN OWNERSHIP POLICIES TO ACHIEVE HIGH EMPLOYMENT THROUGH DEVELOPMENT OF SECONDARY MANUFACTURING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague from Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) was making a very valid point on federal tax policy when his time ran out at about ten minutes to nine o'clock. One conspicuous example is the fact that current Canadian tax policy, as opposed to U.S. tax policy, makes it far easier for an American company to acquire control of a Canadian company than for one Canadian company to acquire control of a second Canadian company. To be specific, American companies and other foreign-owned companies are allowed by their governments to deduct as a business expense the interest paid on money which they borrow to acquire Canadian companies. This is obviously so unfair and so advantageous in particular to the American companies that at the present time the figures show 75 per cent foreign ownership in some fields of Canadian industry.
That is not the whole story by any means. But if we are serious in our desire to regain control of industries which we have already developed, and if we hope to
Measures to Improve Economy
have Canadian control of other industries which we hope to encourage, then a serious tax change has to be made and made now. This motion suggests immediate, emergency measures. Unfortunately, it is too late to do anything very dramatic or sudden this year. But for goodness sake let us start now. It is never too late to mend. It is never too late to start taking control of your own house.
I think that a government which has talked so much about participatory democracy should do something about participation by our own people in the wealth of our own country. I am shocked and amazed that any government which calls itself Liberal, in the old Glad-stone-Laurier sense, should argue that any level of unemployment is acceptable to the Canadian people. I do not often praise Soviet Russia, but I understand that at the present time Russia is seeking to recruit unemployed people from the European labour markets. If these people have skills, Russians are offering them jobs and good opportunities, with good wages which they can take back home in gold. But here in the upper half of North America, the richest half of North America, the undeveloped half of North America we sit around and mostly worry about sharing government jobs and government hand-outs of one form or another.
We have a Department of Industry which, by a stroke of the pen, is able to hand out as much as $12 million to any entrepreneur who seeks help. That sounds fine if it were not coming from a schizophrenic government. What is the good of it offering $12 million to start an entrepreneurial business and then putting out a white paper on taxation which says that in five years it will take a quarter back, in ten years it will take half back and within a generation it will want the whole darn works? Nobody is going to invest money, time, energy or education in the future of a country which offers nothing better than state control.
State control has never worked for the little people. It has not worked in Soviet Russia nor in Czechoslovakia. It is not working in Red China today. They tried it in agriculture, but it did not work. At a time when the Russians and Chinese are giving land back to the peasants, we are rushing through Bill C-176 which is trying to do exactly the reverse, forcing the people of Canada to give up their land to a supposedly all-knowing and capable government, but a government which is floundering with unemployment figures approaching 7 per cent and in local communities with unemployment running a great deal higher than that-up to 10 per cent, 12 per cent and 14 per cent.
The big excuse used by the government is inflation. Mr. Speaker, we have been living with inflation for 20 years and by and large it has done us proud. By inflation we are able to have a two-car garage, get a bigger mortgage and live in a better house. At least that is the case for those who have jobs. But tonight I wish to concentrate on unemployment because it is our big problem.
In some cases I think we have academically overeducated our young people. They are coming out of school in the hundreds of thousands and they want to

May 18, 1971
Measures to Improve Economy participate in the economy. But what are we offering them-soup kitchens, bread-lines, hostels, walking tours of Europe! And when they go to Europe they will find that Europeans are fully employed. When they return they will want to know why they cannot have the same. I think we must have full employment. I think we can achieve it. I agree with the motion when it stresses urgency. It is something we should tackle today.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) returns from Soviet Russia, I hope he will have a satchel full of ideas, not communistic ideas but North American ideas, entrepreneurial ideas to put every Canadian back to work on his own land or in his own business, using a tax policy which means that 20 years from now a man's life will be richer and happier, without him bequeathing unemployment to his children and having them sit around on Parliament Hill or on the Mall growing hair and whining.
Let us be realistic about this, Mr. Speaker. My taxes are high enough but I am willing to be taxed a little more if a 10 per cent increase in my taxes will give jobs to young people. These young people have gone to work in our education system, although in many cases I do not think it is worth a damn. Now they are emerging as PhDs, or as master mechanics from our technical schools and we are telling them that we have nothing for them to do. And all this is at a time when we have only one decent road running east and west across the country, with no decent road running north and south.
We have no transportation into the Arctic worth talking about. We have no idea of the wealth of our natural resources, but our greatest natural resource is our young people. All we are saying to them is that some day things will get better in the American economy and then we will catch up. In effect we are waiting for the American economy to recover, hoping to ride on its wave of prosperity and, incidentally, in the meantime letting the Americans defend us from all the assaults of our enemies. Yet according to my friends to the left we should not accept American money or American investment.
Now I hear a chorus coming from the government benches that we ourselves should own Canada. But they do not have a policy to bring this about. My colleague from Calgary North suggested a tax policy to them. Make it pay to save money. Make it specific. Invest in Canada. Trade is the answer. It is trade that gives us jobs. Only by trade can you set up a business and have something to sell. It is no good setting up a business if you do not have markets.
We need a proper fiscal policy. We don't want a floating dollar. We want to know where the dollar should be pegged to put Canada back into the markets of the world. There is no single commodity in Canada, be it natural or manufactured, which does not benefit from a dollar pegged well below the American dollar. When we had the 92J-cent dollar we flourished. That was supposed to be the biggest mistake that Mr. Diefenbaker's government made; but it was the 92J cent dollar which put this country into the ten years of greatest prosperity we have ever seen. We had better decide now where we want the dollar pegged, or it will rise to U.S. $1.10.
I was also shocked to hear the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) say that the GNP was so high that we did not have to worry any more. This makes me ask the question: Who is making the money? Let us find out. If they are making so much money, then let us create jobs for our own people, and not only for the young people. There are many middle-aged and old people who need jobs. You cannot live on the old age pension today. Where can you live on $100 a month?
The universality of the old age pension makes me laugh. If you build a little shack and manage to save $5,000 in 40 years of work, then the supplement is cut off and you are expected to live on $80 a month. Talk about beating inflation! Are we beating it with the 42 cents given to the old people? That is all we have done in the last five years, give them 40 cents a week which would not even buy a good cigar-maybe seven six-cent stamps to write your Member of Parliament, maybe six seven-cent stamps; I leave it to the Minister of Finance to work that out.
What are our human resources? I suggest that because we are so ignorant about our natural and human resources we should put a couple of hundred thousand young people to work to find out what is our future and their future. I have faith that this country is worth developing. I have faith that the answer to our economic problems is not to sit around and wait for the Americans to solve them. The answer is to create jobs for our young people. They have the brains, the youth and the skill, and it is up to us to give them leadership. I believe that the few who are sitting around growing long hair are far outnumbered by the fine young people who have spent four or five years in high school or college to prepare themselves for the working world, for a bigger and better Canada. I do not think this government is big enough to handle the job.

If the people on the other side of the House cannot do it, then I say call in the young people and let us survey our natural resources, our human resources, our technical resources, our fiscal resources-you name it. Put them to work, and now.
We have wasted two months already. I expect it would take another month to put them to work, but let's do it. Then let us see that when they come out of school next year we have a comprehensive plan which will mean that
rMr. Bigg.]

we are out looking for the labour markets of the world to help us carry on the ideas we have formed in this chamber. If we do not start here it is no good looking to the colleges, to Sparks Street Mall or the United States of America.
The problems of Canada Eire supposed to be solved in this chamber; that is what we are here for. If this government thinks it is incapable of doing it, if they can cynically state that we can stand 10 per cent unemployment in a vibrant and young country like this, then they have no alternative but to resign. I have confidence in the ideas of this party, Mr. Speaker. We can develop Canadian trade and have policies from coast to coast, with none of this divisive business. subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR ECONOMIC MEASURES, PLANNED INVESTMENT AND FOREIGN OWNERSHIP POLICIES TO ACHIEVE HIGH EMPLOYMENT THROUGH DEVELOPMENT OF SECONDARY MANUFACTURING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I listened to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in recent weeks and to the minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) today I could not help thinking of them as characters in Alice in Wonderland-the worse things get, the more they shout that things are better and better.
In April, 1970, Canada had 544,000 people unemployed, and in April of this year unemployment had risen to 659,000, an increase of 20 per cent. If you compare April,
1970,	with April, 1971, you see that in Quebec unemployment rose from 203,000 in April, 1970, to 234,000 this year; in Ontario, unemployment rose from 145,000 in April, 1970, to 205,000 in April this year; in the Maritimes it rose from 66,000 in April, 1970, to 75,000 in April this year; in British Columbia it rose from 58,000 in April, 1970, to 72,000 in April this year.
If you look at the seasonally adjusted rates of unemployment for the last five years, which the Minister of Finance keeps telling us are looking better all the time, you see that there has been a steady increase. In April, 1967, the rate was 4 per cent; in April, 1968, the rate was 4.9 per cent; in 1969 the rate was 4.9 per cent; in 1970 the rate was 5.6 per cent, and this year the rate is 6.7 per cent. In Ontario, the wealthiest province in this country, the seasonally adjusted rate for unemployment in April,
1971,	was 5.7 per cent, the highest in the last ten years.
The unemployment which we are experiencing is not
an accident, Mr. Speaker. Canada has the highest unemployment rate of any country in the western industrial world. In Great Britain, the rate of unemployment has just gone over 3 per cent, and in last week's local elections the Conservatives lost over 2,000 seats. The election was fought on national issues and the people spoke out.
Our unemployment was brought about by a conscious decision of this government. In December, 1969, the Prime Minister said that he would not be deflected from the fight against inflation even if the result was that we
Measures to Improve Economy faced 6 per cent unemployment. The government cut back on programs and called on provincial and municipal governments to follow suit. It tried to implement a policy of voluntary restraints on wages and salaries but, of course, not on profits.
The fight against inflation was temporarily successful. Last year the cost of living rose by less than 2 per cent, but the result was precisely what the New Democratic Party in Parliament, and economists outside, had predicted-higher unemployment. As most economists predicted when the government implemented its policy of restraints, the increase in the cost of living could only be slowed down temporarily. I know of no economist, except some of the trained seals working for the government, who seriously argued that inflation could be stopped in Canada when costs were going up in the United States. After all, we sell most of our products to the United States and we import more from them than from any other country. It is almost impossible, Mr. Speaker, to keep prices in Canada from rising if they are doing so in the United States.
The inevitable happened, as had been predicted by everyone but the government. In the first four months of 1971 the cost of living rose by 1.8 per cent, an annual rate of 5.4 per cent. The Minister of Finance has suggested that this is only temporary and that the increase will slow down. There is no reason to believe that. The price war the supermarkets engaged in last year has disappeared. The temporary help we obtained by unpegging the dollar cannot be repeated. Therefore, costs in Canada will go up this year, as I have suggested.
Now we have the worst of all possible worlds, high unemployment and an increasing rate of inflation. The result of the government's policy has brought tragedy to tens of thousands of Canadians individually and to the provinces and municipalities. Some of the most highly-trained Canadian citizens cannot get jobs. Today, the Toronto Telegram predicts a long job hunt for many of the University of Toronto's 5,700 graduates. A survey undertaken by that newspaper shows that only 40 per cent of this year's engineering graduate class will find jobs at this time, whereas last year 85 per cent of the graduating class at this time of year had found jobs.
Today's Toronto Star reports Quebec Labour Minister Cournoyer as saying that Quebec's welfare recipients have increased by more than 500 per cent in the ten years between 1960 and 1969. They increased from 22,500 in 1960 to 114,3000 in 1969. At the same time, those receiving unemployment insurance declined from 139,000 in 1960 to
101,000	in 1969. The decline in the number of people receiving unemployment insurance in Quebec is not the result of lower unemployment in that province. As I said earlier, they are suffering from higher unemployment than ever before. In that province a tremendously large number of people have been unemployed for so long that they have used up all their unemployment insurance benefits. The figures for April, 1971, ought to have a sobering effect even on this government, for they show that 152,000 people have been unemployed for more than
5938

May 18, 1971
Measures to Improve Economy
six months and that 190,000 people have been unemployed for between four and six months. That increase is startling when one compares it with the number of people who were unemployed for four months or more in other years.
We call on the government to stop its insane preoccupation with inflation, which is a worldwide phenomenon which cannot be prevented and cannot be slowed up very much in one country, and to concentrate on implementing a policy of full employment. The NDP government of Manitoba has not only given this type of advice to the federal government at Ottawa but has implemented the kinds of policies to which I have referred. In February of this year 22,000 people were unemployed in Manitoba, the rate of unemployment being 6 per cent of the labour force. Between February and April of this year unemployment in Manitoba was reduced. It went from 22,000 in February to 18,000 in April. The rate of unemployment dropped from 6 per cent in February to 4.8 per cent in April. That trend has not been duplicated in any other province of this country.
It is no accident that that happened. It come about because the government of Manitoba rejected the idea that it ought to or could combat inflation. The government of Manitoba has taken the position that its objective is 'full employment. When they talk of full employment they talk about the 3 per cent unemployment level referred to in the report of the Economic Council of Canada. Last week the government of Manitoba proposed an expansionary budget designed to provide increased employment of people and resources in the province. The total estimated expenditures for the 1971 fiscal year are over $500 million. For the fiscal year 1971 that government plans a deficit on capital account of an estimated $300 million over and above ordinary revenues. They propose to invest large sums of money in housing, in the expansion of hydro facilities and in the expansion of telephone facilities.
The government of Manitoba has planned a massive public housing program for 1971. They propose to spend $33 million. They had intended spending over $50 million but the federal government would not co-operate and they therefore propose to spend, as I said, $33 million. This is still the largest amount in Manitoba's history, representing an increase of 154 per cent in public housing spending as compared with 1970. The number of housing units involved is in excess of 2,200, representing an increase of 107 per cent from 1970 and almost 1,000 per cent from 1969.
This is the kind of program we have been advocating ever since the government proposed curing the ills of this country by concentrating on the fight against inflation. We have proposed that the government should, instead, make its No. 1 priority full employment. This could be done if the government stopped talking about tax reform and got on with the job of introducing tax legislation which will do away with the inequitable, regressive and inefficient tax system we have at present.
We have proposed that the government adopt tax policies which will put the burden of taxation on those who
can afford to pay. We believe that a more equitable tax structure must be achieved by all levels of government and must be based as much as possible on ability to pay. May I say, in a practical way, that we need to increase income tax exemptions to $2,000 for single persons and $4,000 for married persons.
In the budget which the minister proposes to bring down one month from now we ought to reduce the taxes paid by people in lower income brackets. We ought to be thinking very seriously of increasing old age pensions. We ought to think in a practical way about beginning to put into operation the kinds of projects which are needed so badly in this country. We ought to think about a massive increase in public housing such as has been begun in Manitoba. We ought to think about helping schools and universities acquire new buildings and equipment which they need. We ought to think seriously about helping the provinces and municipalities to deal effectively for the first time with the pollution of air and the pollution of water, and to eliminate it.
There is not one municipality in Canada which does not have inadequate sewage disposal facilities and which does not need to put the squeeze on industries which pollute the air. If one goes no more than 100 yards from this very building one will see how badly the Ottawa River has been polluted. Asking the city of Ottawa or the city of Hull to do the job by themselves is asking for the impossible. The government at Ottawa, Mr. Speaker, ought to take the lead through grants and loans to enable the provinces and municipalities to work on the tremendously important task of turning this corner and to enable them to meet the problems of inflation. If we begin to do these things, we will stop the kind of unemployment we have experienced up until now.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon and evening we have listened to many reasons why the government feels it has acted in a proper manner. They tried to justify the Prime Minister's expression last fall when he said, "Push me and see how far I will go" and when he said that 6 per cent did not seem to be an unreasonable unemployment figure if it meant curtailing inflation.
Almost every country has a higher rate of inflation than Canada, but no country is paying the same penalty. Many of my colleagues have referred to the expense involved in people not working and the hardship it creates. But there will be a long-term problem with which we will have to live. I refer to the young people who are entering the labour market and are unable to find work. These young people will be discouraged before they even get started. The old adage may be true-if you keep a person on welfare for a period of time, that will probably be the pattern for the rest of his life. It may well be that we are creating a situation with which we will have to live for a very long time.
I was in northern Ontario this week. I found that the unemployment figures being used really do not apply to
[Mr. Orlikow.l
May 18, 1971

that part of the country. The actual unemployment figure is very close to 25 per cent. I am not referring to the seasonally adjusted figure, the Canadian average or the Ontario average. If 25 per cent are unemployed, the other 75 per cent will have to carry them.. This means that as soon as the seasonal benefits of unemployment insurance cease, the municipalities will be carrying the welfare load for many years.
It has been pointed out that the city of Ottawa will have a great deal of difficulty fitting the high cost of snow removal into its budget for several years. No doubt the cost of snow removal is high, but think of a municipality where 25 per cent of the wage earners are going to apply for assistance. It is true that the municipality will only pay 20 per cent of the cost, but in many areas where employment has been poor for several years this will bankrupt them.
I listened to the Prime Minister on television the other night. It was pointed out that the interview had been taped prior to delivery and was several weeks old. I suggest that the broadcast was several months old. The subjects and the discussion were months old. The program was taped before this calamity affected many of our communities. At the time it was taped, it could still be argued that we could economically afford to curtail unemployment, building, development and secondary industry, all for the sake of curtailing inflation.
Surely all the economists in the government are not archaic. Some should be table to tell the government that in other countries inflation is not a serious problem as long as the gross national product increases to the same degree or more. I agree that it costs more money to purchase commodities, but there is more money available. What advantage is there in the person who has been unemployed for seven or eight months knowing that if we are able to keep him out of work, we are able to cut down on the niceties of life and that a television set or drugs will cost less? He knows that the only place he can get money to buy food and pay rent is the welfare office. You can be holier than thou in terms of inflation but you cannot be holier than thou with regard to the needs of these people.
Another budget is going to be brought down. Until I heard some of the government members today I would have predicted that we could not possibly operate for another year with old age pension recipients paying income tax. I was sure this mess would have been straightened out so that we would not ask an old age pensioner receiving a guaranteed supplement to pay $70 income tax out of one of his monthly cheque. Something should be done for the man carrying the lunchpail who is still employed, so that his lot will be better and he will have a little more money to distribute and will enjoy the same purchasing power as the top one-third of the country. If I understood the government members correctly, they said that if you spread the load and give a concession across the board, this would be inflationary. They said he would spend the money, and you cannot give him a reduction.

Canadians will not forget that this is not an emergency that has arisen, it is not a calamity that affects the nation, nor is it something that is happening in Europe. They will not forget that this is not happening in other countries. The situation in Canada today, with more unemployment than we have seen for many years, is a creation of the government which intentionally set out to have 6, 7 or 8 per cent of the people unemployed. The Canadian people will not forget that they have been made the tools of a government which is not interested in the welfare of the average Canadian but is more interested in those clipping bonds coupons, living on insurance benefits and enjoying the niceties that many of the working people have been unable to afford even in good times. In all humanity, this government will have to consider its citizens and make adjustments in the budget to put Canada back in the employment field, rather than on the welfare rolls.

subsubtopic: FINANCE-USE OF PORTION OF REVENUE FROM ALCOHOL TO COMBAT ALCOHOLISM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question tonight is: Is consideration being given at the federal level to providing an amount of money, possibly a percentage of federal liquor revenues, toward combating alcoholism and promoting temperance in Canada? As hon. members know, the province of Prince Edward Island and the province of British Columbia have recently moved toward this goal, but what is the federal government doing in this regard? I should like to put a few figures on the record in this connection. Ottawa takes in rather more than $1 million a day as its share of revenue from the sale of drink-that is, liquor, wine and beer. If we include the federal government sales tax, revenue from liquor totals close to $400 million a year.
What does Ottawa spend, having made this immense amount out of the sale of alcohol, on preventing people from becoming alcoholics or on educating young people particularly against the acceptance of drinking, or at least of overdrinking? It spends little or nothing, Mr. Speaker. It is true that the federal government shares in projects of health and welfare with the provinces and that some of this money goes in providing aid to alcoholics. But it is not this that I am talking about. What I am urging is that at least one per cent of federal revenue from the sale of liquor-that is to say, approximately $4
5940

May 18, 1971
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion million a year-be directed toward promoting temperance and publicizing the health and social problems that are caused by drinking to excess, very much in the same way as the health and welfare department some years ago embarked upon a program to educate young people against starting to smoke cigarettes.
It is not as though the federal government could not afford to earmark some of the revenue obtained from the drink trade for this purpose. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, that more than half of a bottle of whisky consists of water? Do you know that $5 out of each $6 bottle of whisky represents taxes? Canadians are actually drinking watered taxes. Even so, the result is tragic in many thousands of homes, families and businesses. As one who helped instigate the breathalyzer legislation, I know that the 15 per cent drop in fatal accidents since the advent of that law means that there are 760 Canadians alive today who otherwise would have been in the graveyard during the first year of application of the breathalyzer law.
The loss caused by alcoholism to Canadian industry and business is estimated to be $325 million a year, manifesting itself in multimillion dollar hangovers. There can be no estimate of the loss to Canada, caused by alcoholism, in broken homes and in rising crime. I raised this question some time ago and was told that Ottawa made a total grant of $15,000 a year to the Canadian Foundation on Alcoholism. A few days ago the minister of health told me that the government has no stated formal program in regard to combating alcoholism, though he said-and it is true-that Ottawa shares funds with the provinces, some of which go to assist victims of alcoholism. But, Mr. Speaker, I am not trying to get at this question. What I want the government to say tonight is what its attitude is to setting up a fund consisting of, say, one per cent of its annual income from the sale of liquor, which money would go to educating people against alcoholism, to preventing alcoholism-not to bind up the wound but to stop the wound from developing in the first place.
The federal government takes in $1 million a day in revenue from the sale of drink. When the sale of liquor promotes social ills, broken homes, death and disease I think it is the duty of the government to set aside some amount from its revenue from such sale in order to combat alcoholism and to educate people, particularly the young people, against the use of alcohol. My question is: Will the government consider setting up such a program, providing funds for the program and encouraging interprovincial action with the federal authority to combat alcoholism in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, the suggestion that all or a portion of a given tax source be earmarked for a particular expenditure is not uncommon. What it means is that a particular revenue item would be committed in advance to pay in whole or in part for a specific program. The specific program is invariably of the of unassailable virtue and unquestionable merit.
Notwithstanding the allure, the idea involves the abdication by Parliament of its control over spending. The
funds for a designated program would rise and fall with the tax received, without regard to the relative costs or public desirability of the program; Parliament would not have to consider that. The tax revenue once earmarked would automatically flow to the designated program, and to that extent Parliament would be relieved of its direct right and obligation to determine how much the government shall spend and the purposes for which it shall spend it.
The hon. member's suggestion may have some superficial appeal, but recognizing its implications for Parliament the government is not prepared to concur in the denial of the right and obligation of Parliament at each session to vote supply. With respect to the idea of the program itself, I will certainly refer it to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro).

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 17 I asked the following question of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) as recorded in Hansard at page 5858:
I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Labour, Mr. Speaker. It is based on the practice of hiring pipeline welders in Edmonton or Winnipeg only for a Trans-Canada construction job in Saskatchewan, a practice which effectively prevents the hiring of welders from Saskatchewan. Would the minister investigate such hiring procedures and determine whether Saskatchewan welders are not entitled to a fair chance of such job opportunities?
The Minister of Labour replied:
I am not sure if this is a question I can answer adequately. Perhaps it should be directed to the Minister of Manpower. But it seems very likely to be a problem coming within provincial jurisdiction since it concerns hiring arrangements.
I then directed the following supplementary question to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Mar-chand), although it was not permitted at that time:
Could I ask the Minister of Manpower if he has any indication whether any Saskatchewan welders could be hired for work on this project?
Mr. Speaker, Majestic Construction Limited of Edmonton has a $55 million contract for a pipeline from Bur-stall to Moosomin, in the province of Saskatchewan. This is with regard to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited. The welders belong to the International Brotherhood of Plumbers and Pipefitters. However, the hiring on jobs from Swift Current west is under the jurisdiction of the Edmonton hiring office, and the hiring from Swift Current east is under the jurisdiction of the Winnipeg hiring office.
It appears that this problem should have been resolved long ago by the union itself. There should have been hiring from the province of Saskatchewan in order that the welders in that province who qualify could have been hired at that hiring hall. I assure you that there appears to be no excuse for hiring practices such as are being carried on by this union. However, I believe the greatest challenge we have before us is in relation to the danger of balkanization of various provinces.

May 18, 1971

Many provincial governments are acting or reacting in such a way that they can do nothing but harm to this nation. We are fast approaching a situation where there will be ten provinces, each passing legislation denying the entry of anyone from another province to work within its borders. We have already heard words from Quebec that manpower should be under provincial legislation. We know what has happened in Quebec. They have suggested that construction workers should be hired from Quebec only, and that people from provinces other than Quebec should not be permitted to work on construction jobs there.
We also hear from British Columbia that government people are suggesting that only B.C. workers should be employed on any project within that province. A typical example was seen recently in Prince George where some Saskatchewan people went to obtain employment. Employment was available, but when they said they came from Saskatchewan they were told that only British Columbia people were being hired. We also hear that people in the province of Alberta are suggesting that people from Saskatchewan should go back to Saskatchewan rather than come into Alberta for job opportunities. We have to ask ourselves, where we are going with this type of provincial barrier?
We listened to the chicken and egg debate in this House of Commons concerning the movement of produce from one province to another. We now have a provincial immigration war going on across our nation. No better example could be used than having the Minister of Labour pass the ball to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang) in respect of this question. Surely the present pipeline contract over which this dispute arose was public knowledge for some time. This is what the Minister of Labour for Saskatchewan indicated in a press release:
I wish to make it known, in the bluntest of terms, that the government demands Saskatchewan residents be hired for work undertakings in the province. If this policy is not adhered to immediately, we will take whatever action is needed to facilitate its prompt and effective implementation.
Surely that Minister of Labour knew about the $55 million contract, if he wanted to set down guidelines for the hiring of Saskatchewan welders. I ask the parliamentary secretary whether his department intends to allow Canada to become a country of ten nations, or whether the federal government intends to get the ten Premiers together to bring sense and reason to bear on the real problem facing our nation at the present time.
There is no reason for having a Department of Labour or a Department of Manpower if each province makes its
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion own decision. The relocation grant will mean little if this is to continue and if each of the Premiers of the ten provinces are to set up their own little empires and hire only within their provinces. With regard to the contractor to whom I referred who refused to hire Saskatchewan welders, the union and the provincial government can only be held responsible for the situation which has developed in the province. Unless the federal government immediately moves on this serious problem in Saskatchewan and also in respect of each of the ten provinces in Canada, we will no longer be a nation.
I believe it is important that the parliamentary secretary attempt to answer tonight whether or not the department he represents will try to do something to bring about understanding among the ten provinces of Canada with respect to hiring practices. I am positive that unless understanding is brought about within the departments of labour in each of the ten provinces in Canada, we will become balkanized and a country of ten nations, which is something we must avoid at all costs.

subsubtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-FAILURE TO HIRE SASKATCHEWAN WELDERS FOR PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION PROJECT IN PROVINCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would seem that the concern of the hon. member is at two levels, one short-term and one a long-range solution. Evidently, if the hon. member is looking for a quick solution to the question the most effective place for the matter to be raised would be in the legislature of Saskatchewan. He has admitted that this issue comes under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments.
We have information to the effect that the collective agreements in connection with the pipeline construction project give jurisdiction over welders on this project to the Plumbers and Pipefitters Locals 254 in Winnipeg and 488 in Edmonton, and that other workers are under the jurisdiction of union locals in Saskatchewan. We also understand that pending settlement of negotiations between the plumbers and pipefitters locals in Winnipeg and Edmonton and the local in Regina, work on the pipeline will not commence.
Regarding the long-range issue that the hon. member is raising, as to whether provincial governments should or should not have jurisdiction on labour relations, as they now have for specific sectors, of course this would be a question that could be raised at any federal-provincial constitutional conference. But if a satisfactory solution to this specific issue or to similar issues is to be found within the context of the present Constitution, I would suggest that the approximate place for raising the question is in the respective provincial legislatures, and the hon. member knows that.
At 10.20 p.m. the House adjourned, without question put, pursuant to Standing Order.
